column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The desc's Pictish province of Circinn is not in the article; not repeated. 'Mearns' etymology from A' Mhaoirne 'the stewartry' given in plain words.
Article: Hideaki later renamed himself again with different characters (秀詮) after Sekigahara; left out as only a change of characters.

Article gives 1878 for East Griqualand passing to the Cape Colony; the entry says 1879: year left out. Article says Kok settled here in 1863; entry says the town was founded in 1869: 1863 left out, the 1869 mission kept as the article gives it.

Article calls it the second-highest mine in the world, behind Yanacocha; softened to 'one of the highest' to avoid a ranking. The entry's 2022 full ownership is not in the article. The article does not say how Centerra Gold came to hold the mine after Cameco; left out.
Article gives 1987 for the find; the entry says 1989: year left out. The article also has the first translation in 1991 and 'a year later' after the find; the years of the translation left out.

The entry says he built up lands around Leuven and Brussels; the article says it is unclear whether Brussels came to him in his lifetime (Van Droogenbroeck: only later generations). Brussels left out of the text.
Article gives the distance from Rome as 6 km; the entry says about 30 km: distance left out. Article's 'numerous altars' used; the entry's thirteen altars not repeated.
Article: deployed at Legio (León) in AD 74; entry says from Vespasian's reign, consistent. Year 74 not printed to keep the text simple.
Entry says earl from about 1030; article says some time before 1032: no year printed.
Present-day figures (assets, staff) left out as 'as of' figures.
Article: amnesty granted 1842, return to Montreal 1845; the entry's 'returning after an amnesty in 1845' could be read as an 1845 amnesty, so no amnesty year is printed and the return is not dated.

Article dates the governorship 1949-1965 (took office 2 January 1949); entry says elected in 1948, consistent. The entry's 'poet' is supported only by the book Borrones and Kennedy's citation; not repeated.

Population share and the Gurkha recruiting in Singapore etc. left out. The People's War paragraph of the article is partisan in tone ('most significant and historic role', 'renowned for their bravery'); only plain facts kept.
Article dates his death to February 1316, perhaps 11 February if he ruled 35 days; the entry's d. 1316 agrees.

Article's figures of 70,000-100,000 Afghans massacred in 1585-86 and 8,000-40,000 Mughal dead are unsourced in tone and left out. The article dates his Kabul governorship 1585-1586 in the lead but has him appointed after the 1581 annexation; no dates printed for it.

The article gives his marriage to Felicia Orsini both as May 1552 and as 29 April 1552; only the year is given. Left out his later residence at L'Aquila, which could read as contradicting the entry's viceroyalty until his death.
Short article (about 420 words); the presidency's reforms are already in the entry, so the text adds his Guatemalan career and the library.

The article dates his reign c. 1095–1078 BC; the entry gives c. 1099–1082 BCE. No reign dates are printed. The entry names the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I and the town Ekallatum; the text uses the article's forms Tukultī-apil-Ešarra and Ekallāte. The article spells the astrologer both Ea-mušallim and Ea-mušillim.

The entry gives d. c. 963; the article says died before 963, and reports Brzozowska and Leszka's view that she may have died as early as the beginning of the 960s or even before 958. The text gives only that the year is unknown and that 963 is the latest possible date; the earlier possibilities are left out. Career is an odd heading for a consort; the marriage is the only public act the article records.

The article says Katataka died in early 1852 and Katamori succeeded at 18, which does not fit his birth in 1836 or his marriage in 1856; no year of succession is given. The coup is given as 30 September (or 18 August by the old calendar); no year is printed, as the article gives none.
The article says he died aged 67, which does not fit his dates (1753–1818); no age is given.

Figures for those killed in the movement's protests vary in the article between 30 and 200; only the count for Nanjing Road itself is given. The article's aftermath section mixes events from before 30 May (meetings of 28 May, Ku Cheng-hung) with later ones; it was not used for the sequence.

Their share of Rajasthan's population is given by different reports as 7%, 10% and 14%; left out. Present-day disputes over reservations (the Gurjar question, media claims about shares of benefits) left out as not lasting facts.

The article places the army's transformation under his chancellorship (from 1677); the entry says he began the reform as secretary for war. The text names the army reform without tying it to either office. Short article (about 500 words).
The article writes the recapture as '1031-1031'; given as 1031.

The article credits him as architect of the Shah Mosque in Isfahan, with acoustic calculations; left out as doubtful and unsourced in the article. The article's family section includes a garbled list of descendants and a line on Ali Khamenei; left out. About 290 words: the article has little beyond the entry.
The article says he was deported in 1862 after the Convention of Scutari; the entry says he fought in the war of 1862. Both can be true; the exile is given as the article has it.

The entry says a British company controlled the mines from 1889; the article gives only the expedition of 1886, so no date of company control is printed. Kyat Pyin and Kyatpyin are both spellings in the article.
Short article (about 400 words). The entry says its origins lie in the 10th century or earlier; the article gives a building date of 920 for the old monastery, which fits.

The entry dates the Jarrow foundation around 681–82; the article gives 684–5 in its lead, a royal grant of land in 682 and the establishment of St Paul's in 685, with the church dedicated on 23 April 685. No Jarrow foundation year is printed. The article dates the World Heritage nomination both 2011 and 2012; no year is printed.

The article's lead calls him prince of Tmutarakan and Chernigov, which its biography does not explain; left out. Alexander Nevsky's mother is not named in the article; the text says only 'through his daughters'. His daughter Rostislava married Yaroslav II of Vladimir, who appears in the biography as Yaroslav of Suzdal.
The article says Majlesi held a teaching certificate from Mulla Sadra while opposing Mulla Sadra's school; both are given as stated.

SKIPPED: different subject: the saved article is about al-Zagal (c. 1440–1494), Boabdil's uncle and rival, not Boabdil The article titled Muhammad XII of Granada describes al-Zagal, reigning 1485–1487, and calls Boabdil Muhammad XI. The entry is Boabdil (Muhammad XII, c. 1460–1533). Its confirmed article should be checked (entry-wikidata-manual.tsv).

The article says Baekje 'tried to attack' its northern boundary 'notably in 505'; worded as an attack in 505. Heungan and Boyeon are listed as sons; the article also calls Anjang the eldest son, so they are given as two other sons.

The entry calls Istami his brother; the article calls Istami his uncle. Istami is named without a relation. The article's lead calls him a son of Illig Qaghan and its biography a son of Bumin Qaghan; no father is named.

The article gives the length of the resistance as fifty-three days; the entry says 'some seven weeks'. I wrote only 'from July to September 1915'. The 2016 film The Promise and the chief priest's quotation left out.

The article gives his birth as 603; the entry has only 'd. 661', so I left the birth year out. The article's own story mixes Bohee/Bo-hee and Munhee/Mun-hee spellings; I used Munhee. Marriage story framed as a story since the article gives no source for it.

The article is short; three sections written mostly from its history and performance sections, with the lyrics summarised in Contents. Kelly Clarkson at the second Obama inauguration left out for length.

The article calls him a Russian Bolshevik; the entry a Ukrainian Bolshevik. I used neither label. The article says both 'Commissar of Education of the USSR' and head of the Ukrainian Commissariat of Education from 1927; I wrote only 'head of education from 1927'.

The article gives his death as 9 September 1868 in the lead and 5 September 1868 later; I wrote only 'September 1868'. The entry places the move onto the plateau 'around 1840'; the article says he settled in Matabeleland in 1840, which agrees.

The article places Nakbe about 13 km 'south' of El Mirador; the entry says south-east. Direction left out. The article says villages were levelled 'around 1200 BC' for platform foundations but also dates monumental architecture to the 8th century BC; I gave no date for the levelling. The article dates its collapse to the Terminal Formative (100-200 CE) in the lead but says it was never a major centre after the start of the Late Preclassic; left the collapse date out. The article spells the project both RAINPEG and RAINPEC; I used RAINPEG.
Rendered 'roughly 5 to 6 miles' as 'some miles'. The 2006 selection among Japan's 100 Most Famous Castles and the cherry blossoms left out.
The article dates his rule as amir from 865; the entry says he governed from Samarkand from 875. Start date left out. Short article (about 450 words of substance): three short sections.

The article gives the cabinet both as 16 appointed ministers and as 15 cabinet members in a 65-seat house; I wrote only that the constitution limits the cabinet to 16. The article's 2024 turnout line left out.

The article says the Supreme Court ruled in February 2010; I wrote 'the case was decided in the service's favour' to avoid naming a court the article may have wrong. The channel's present depth and deepening project left out (written as ongoing). The article does not mention the Caddo heartland or the 1690 missions in the entry; nothing about them added.
Short article; two sections. Quotations are the stela's words as the article gives them. The entry gives no throne-order; Ryholt/Baker's 'third or fourth' added as attributed.
'German forces in western Africa' in the article; I wrote 'in the region'. Short article; every point used.

The article dates parts of the banqueting hall to the 13th century and the castle to the 15th; the entry calls the hall 15th-century. I gave no date for the hall. The article also calls the town 'the second-largest urban center in the county'; consistent with 'largest town apart from Limerick city'.
The article says the fighting devastated 'Jiangsu and Hunan'; Hunan lies outside the Nian region, so I left the provinces out. Hudson and den Boer's 'bare branches' argument left out for length.

The entry says Niccolò ruled Reggio from 1409; the article does not mention Reggio. The article says he named Borso heir in 1429; the entry says three of his sons succeeded him, and the article does not say who succeeded first. Left out so the page does not seem to disagree with itself.

The article gives his death as 24 March 1943 in the lead and 4 March 1943 in the biography; I wrote only 'March 1943'. The article says he fled Russia with British help; the entry says he was expelled abroad. I wrote only 'left Russia by way of Vladivostok'. The article spells Nietzsche 'Neitszche'; I left the name out. The article calls him a founder and first chairman of the PSR, which I left out as doubtful.

The article places the subsidiary alliance 'the following year' after 1795; the entry dates it 1798. No date given. The article calls him the 5th Nizam; left out. The article's comparison of Hyderabad with the United Kingdom left out.
The entry dates the failed Sasanian siege to 551; the article gives only the war of 540-562, which agrees.

The article's lead says he became party leader in 1964 but its body says he became party president in 1964 and challenged Nordmeyer at the end of 1965; I used only the 1965 challenge. The entry's recognition of the People's Republic of China is not in the article; not mentioned.

The precise function of the determiner -(i)l is disputed (some scholars treat it as a nominative or subject marker); I called it a determiner, as the article concludes. Dotawo, named in the entry, is not in the article.
The entry says Lula's convictions were later annulled; the saved excerpt mentions only his release after a Supreme Court ruling in November 2019, so the annulment is not told here.

The entry has Gregory XIII merging the two orders at Emmanuel Philibert's request; the article says Gregory united Saint Lazarus with the Crown of Savoy and the duke merged it with Saint Maurice. The 1572 merger itself is not retold here. The article says Pius V re-established Saint Maurice in 1572; left out. The entry says the order is conferred by the head of the house of Savoy; the article says that headship and the grand mastership are disputed between two claimants, which is stated without choosing between them.

The entry says Sweden held it from 1612; the article says Sweden captured it in 1611 during the Ingrian War. The year is left out here. The article dates the last prisoners' departure to 6 January 1906 on Yuvachov's word; given as January 1906.

The article says the conflicts began in the 1360s and that Nicopolis is thought to have been the first battle between the two; the entry dates the wars 1366–1526 and the phrase about the 1360s is not used.

The article first says the Venetians built the fort on Kastri and then that it was probably one of the castles built or rebuilt by the Genoese Arrigo da Castello between 1199 and 1218; the builder is left out. The entry says the Minoan town has been excavated since 1902; the article gives no year.
Left out the present-day remarks (Žižek on China, the Turkish flag) as present-day assessment.
The article has little history beyond Pineda's settlement of 1519; the Huastecs and Nuevo Santander of the entry are not in it.
The article says the Pa'O settled in the Thaton region around 1700 BC, without a source in the excerpt; left out as doubtful. The article spells the leaf thanapet; the entry thanaphet.

The article names an earliest known parliament at Kilkea Castle on 18 June 1264 (prelates and magnates only); the entry has the parliament meeting from the late 13th century, so 1264 is left out. The article places Poynings' Law in 1495 in its lead and 1494 in its history section; no year given here. The entry says it passed the Crown of Ireland Act of 1542; the article says Henry VIII declared the kingdom in 1541. Neither year is given here.

The entry says that in 1980 they and the Penobscot won a major land claims settlement; the article says the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 9 September 1980 reduced elements of Passamaquoddy sovereignty and land claims. The act is left out here. The article says the Canadian Passamaquoddy mostly speak French and English; not used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance

The entry gives about 50,000 convicts to the American colonies; the article gives estimates of 50,000 to 120,000. The number is left out here. The entry gives 1788–1868 for Australia; the article says the First Fleet departed in 1787 and transportation continued until 1868. The departure year is used, not an arrival year.

The entry names the colonies Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Connecticut; the article's lead names Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Saybrook and later the Connecticut Colony. The list of colonies is not repeated here.

The entry dates the bombardment of the Majlis to 1908; the article dates it to January 1907. No year is given here. The article says the brigade was commanded by Russian officers until 1920 but also that the British took it over after 1917 and removed the Russian officers; the year of the change of command is left out.
The article says the town served in the 16th century as an outpost of Lan Na; the entry's Tilokarat and the Burmese period are not in the article and are not retold.
The entry puts Fort Maurepas at Biloxi in 1699; the article puts the fort of 1699 at Ocean Springs and has Iberville reaching Biloxi in January 1700. The fort's place is not given here.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance once the property and hotel details are set aside
The article has him appointed consul for 79 BCE by Sulla and also elected; I wrote neither and left the consulship to the description.

The entry calls it the state temple of the Mengwi kingdom; the article calls it a family temple (pura kawiten) of the king's ancestors. Both may hold; I used the article's term without denying the entry's.

The article's Sher Mandal paragraph credits the tower to Babur and Humayun as well as Sher Shah and is confused; left out beyond its name. Humayun's fall (24 January 1556) is in the entry and was not repeated. The article spells the internment camp 'Purana Quila' in a quotation; kept as there.
The article does not mention the Yemeni manuscripts the entry names; nothing on them added.

The article says the castle may have been built by the Numayr but more likely under Salim; not used, as the entry keeps to the Uqaylid holding. The article dates Nur ad-Din's rebuilding from 1168; the entry says 12th century, consistent; not repeated.
The article dates the Arab conquest 636/7; the entry gives 637. Left the date out. Sayf al-Dawla's stand is dated only as three years after 963; written so.

The entry dates his death c. 54 BCE; the article says the late 50s BCE. No death year written. The entry dates the Cretan sieges 69-67 BCE; the article says he took the command after his consulship. The start of the campaign is left undated.

The article has him overseeing the first construction of the Antonine Wall in 143, after the governorship of 139-142 that both it and the entry give. The year 143 is left out. The article's account of the trial is garbled (Ptolemaeus called 'her', accused by her ex-husband); only the bare facts were kept. 'The historian' for Champlin and Wells: the article calls Champlin Professor and names Wells without title.

The entry dates his birth c. 1470; the article gives 1485. No birth year written. The entry says he was murdered at Jamsheed's instigation; the article says Jamsheed assassinated him. Worded so as not to decide.

The article says his reign lasted from 1292 in its lead and 1293 in its heading; the entry gives 1293. No start year for the reign written. Pararaton says Mahisa Campaka was the son of Mahisa Wonga Teleng, son of Ken Arok; written as grandson of Ken Arok.
The article says RTL became majority shareholder of Five from 2006, initial minority shareholder from 1997; written as 'owned ... from 2006'. Could read 'majority owner'.
The entry dates the work 1148-1149; the article says only the 12th century. Not repeated.

The entry's title is 'Duke of Lorraine'; the article says he never appears as duke of Lorraine but did call himself duke. Kept the article's wording, which does not deny the entry's statement that he was recognised as duke or margrave in Lotharingia.
Article dates German South West Africa's Reichskommissar from 7 October 1884 and Nachtigal's Togo tenure 5-6 July 1884; Kamerun 14-19 July 1884.

The entry says the Assyrians executed Rezin; the article says the Bible records his execution, which 'is neither confirmed nor disconfirmed by independent evidence', while also saying the inscriptions have Tiglath-Pileser slay him. His end was not retold.
The article's lead says he was named Justiciar of South Wales in 1171; the body says Henry appointed him 'justice on his behalf in all Deheubarth' shortly after 1172. No year given for the office.

The article does not mention the move of the seat of government after Pepin's attack in 810 or the stone bridge of 1591 given in the entry; nothing here contradicts them. The article spells the building Fabriche Vechie; kept as given.

The article's lead says Robert received Beaumont-le-Roger as an appanage in 1309; its Influence section says Philip VI granted it in June 1328. The date is left out. The article says he forged the will of his 'late father'; the claim to Artois went through his grandfather, so the text says only forgery.
Max Muller / Max Mueller: the article spells the name both ways; kept as given in each place.

The entry's Gulf of Naples battle of 1284 is the Battle of Castellammare of 5 June 1284 in the article. The article does not mention Jerba. Left out his brief service with Edward I of England, told in one sentence in the article.

The article dates Ali Mohammed Khan's Kumaon invasion both 1744 and late 1743; no year given. The article calls Ali Mohammed Khan 'a Jat boy' and also one of two Hindus Daud Khan adopted; the text says only Hindu boys. The article spells him Ali Mohammed and Ali Muhammad; the entry's Ali Mohammed is used.

The article gives no date for the abolition of local tribunals beyond 'the mid 18th century'; left out, as the entry names Tuscany under Peter Leopold. The article's lead says the system was developed 'during the second half of the 16th century' while also giving 1542 as its founding; 1542 used, as in the entry.

One sentence of the article says Corbulo took 'IV Ferrata' to his meeting with Tiridates, apparently a slip for VI Ferrata; legion numbers left out. The article dates the annexations of Pontus and Colchis to 64 and of Commagene and Lesser Armenia to 72; years left out for brevity.

The article gives the play twenty-one acts in its plot section but says Min Qiji's album has an image for each of its twenty acts; the number is left out. The entry dates the work c. 1300; the article places its appearance in the thirteenth century. No date given in the text.

The entry says Rurik sacked Kiev in 1203 'allied with the Olgovichi and the Cumans'; the article names a conflict with the Olgovichi as the cause of his deposition and says he attacked with his kinsmen and a Cuman army. The text names only the Cumans and kinsmen. The article lists Vsevolod Chermny's seizures of Kiev as 1206, 1207 and 1211, though Rurik had abdicated in 1210; years left out. The entry dates his death c. 1212; the article gives 19 April 1212.

The article gives his death year as 603 or, in the Annales Cambriae, 612, and notes 13 January was a Sunday in 603 and 614; the entry has d. c. 614. No year given in the text. The article calls him Archbishop of Strathclyde in one place; left out. The entry spells the king Rhydderch Hael; the article's Riderch Hael is used.

The article's lead gives his death as 28 December 1251 and its biography as 28 November 1251; no day given. The article names Godan's adviser as the Reting abbot (Petech) or the Drigung abbot (J.Y. Chang); the text says only a Tibetan abbot. The entry spells the prince Köten; the article's Godan Khan is used.

The article calls Salomon count of Rennes and Nantes from 852 and duke of Brittany from 857, using the title king intermittently after 868, and quotes a Redon historian that he was king in name only; the entry calls him king from 857. The text speaks of his reign and throne without settling the title. The entry's 'Cotentin and Avranchin' of 867 are the article's counties of Avranches and Coutances; not repeated.

The article does not count the colossal heads or date Stirling's finds of 1945 and 1946; it says he began excavating after a visit in 1938 and that four projects ran from 1946 to 1970. Not repeated. Coe and Diehl's phases (San Lorenzo phase c. 1400-1000 BCE) were left out to avoid a second date range beside the entry's 1400-900 BCE.

The article says the Real Audiencia appointed him interim viceroy in 1807 and that he was officially appointed in May 1808; the entry has viceroy 1807-1809. Consistent; only the 1808 confirmation is mentioned.
The article does not give the year of discovery (1881 in the entry) or a precise date; it says late sixth century BCE, consistent with the entry's c. 520 BCE.
The article spells her patron both Hasan Kucek and Hassan Kuchak; Hasan Kuchak is used, as in the entry. Left out the article's placing of Arzan in Georgia, which looks doubtful.

The article gives his death as 14 September 1923 (lead), 15 September (Career) and 10 September (Death); no day given, as in the entry. The article spells the poet Badie Khayri, Badi' Khayri and Badi' Khairi; Badi' Khairi used for the memoirs as written there.

The article notes some sources give his birth as 914; the entry's 916 is kept and 914 not mentioned. The article gives no single year for the founding of the emirate; the entry's 945 is not repeated or contradicted.

The article mentions the Spartans' leader from Athens without naming Tyrtaeus; he is not named here. The article's claim that Sparta quelled the revolt 'following the death of the Argive commander' was left out: the commander is not otherwise identified.
The article names the historian only as Scullard; no initials added.

The article says he is securely attested between 324 and 312 BCE and that coins have been used to argue he still ruled in 297 BCE, after the entry's c. 300 BCE end; the reign dates are left out of the text. The article names the mound Golyamata Kosmatka, the entry Golyama Kosmatka; the text avoids the name.

The article contradicts itself on who released Shahu in 1707: the lead says Bahadur Shah I, the early-life section Prince Azam Shah. The text names neither. The lead's claims about the Afsharid invasion and Maratha control of Afghanistan and Punjab under Shahu are unsourced in the excerpt and left out.
SKIPPED: article has about 200 words of substance and adds little beyond the description
The article dates the first seaborne raid 'around 1473-3', an evident slip; the text gives no year for it. The article names the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yassar; the entry spells Farrukh Yasar.

The article dates his reign c. 1184-1155 BC (middle chronology), the entry c. 1185-1155 BCE; no reign dates are given in the text. The article does not mention his son Kutir-Nahhunte or the Code of Hammurabi, both in the entry; nothing is said about them.

The article says the Mamluks partly destroyed and then rebuilt the castle and added the long causeway; the entry says they dismantled it after 1291. The text says they partly destroyed and later rebuilt it, with no date, and leaves out who built the causeway. The article does not mention Frederick II, the lords of Sidon or the Templars.

The article has Siemowit receive Belz under the treaty of 12 December 1385, as Alexandra's dowry, and rule it after 1388; the entry says he received Belz as a fief in 1388. The text does not date the grant of Belz. The article gives his birth as c. 1353/1356, the entry c. 1352; no birth year is given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; a longer text would be padded

The article says Vratsian himself became premier of the Republic of Mountainous Armenia; the entry says the republic was led by Garegin Nzhdeh. The text says he became its premier without saying who led it. Oliver Baldwin's account that his son died of exposure on the flight to Persia is left out as a single uncorroborated source.
The article dates his forced resignation 23 December 1345 (and 'six years later'); the entry says he abdicated in 1344. The text gives no year for the resignation.
The article names the Tibetan monastery seized in 1791 as Digarcha in the narrative and refers to goods plundered from Tashilhunpo in the settlement; the text keeps both as the article has them.

The article gives Rana Sanga's reign as 1508-1528 in one place and 1508-1527 in its list; no dates for him are given. The article's list ends the ruling Maharanas in 1947 and begins the titular ones then; the entry says the dynasty ruled Mewar until 1949. The text gives no end date.

The entry calls the episode with Cunizza an affair; the article says he abducted her at her brother's instigation. The text follows the article without calling it an affair, which does not contradict the entry's broader word.
The article speaks of Sosurim's reconciliation policy with Baekje and also of his attacks on Baekje in 374-376; the reconciliation is left out.

The article dates the division of Kamerun to 28 June 1919; the entry dates the polity from 1922. The text gives no year for the division. The article does not say the 1961 plebiscite was in February; no month is given in the text.
The entry's phrase 'democratic republic of workers of all classes' is not in the article; it is not repeated.

The article gives contradictory marriage dates for Elizabeth of Kuyavia (offered 1323, legalized by 1339, married since June 1335); marriages left out except where needed. The article says Stephen 'ceded' Ston and Pelješac to Ragusa in 1333 in agreement with Stefan Dušan, for the tribute of Ston; the entry says 'sold'. Not repeated. Catherine may have been his niece; written as 'relatives'.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance beyond the entry; its painting date (around 1601) also differs from the entry's 1595-1596 Article: paintings 'from around 1601'; entry: painted around 1595-1596.

Entry: besieged Batavia in 1628 and 1629; article mentions an attack 'in 1629' and attempts 'in 1628-1629': no dated sentence used. In 1641 he received an Arabic title from imams in Mecca; left out for length.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (one line of history, census figures and lists of colleges); its elevation (900 m) also differs from the entry's 1,170 m Article: average elevation 900 metres; entry: about 1,170 m.

Historians disagree on why they moved into Maryland in 1675: most cite a Haudenosaunee defeat c. 1674, Francis Jennings argued Maryland coerced them; left out for length. Descendants are among the Seneca-Cayuga Nation and the Six Nations of the Grand River; left out for length.

The article's lead dates the wars to the 12th and 13th centuries, but its body runs to 1445; the entry says 12th-14th century. No overall span given in the text. The 1142 entry of the chronicle is disputed (who the merchants were and who won); told only as disputed.
Al-Bakri described salt mines at a place called Tantatal in 1068 that may be the same; left out for length.

The entry says the forts were built from 1913; the article says the main Taleh fort was built in 1909-1910 (and that most Dervish operated in the Sanaag forts from 1913). Construction dates left out. Article says Carro Seed Magan was the mother of 'the emir of Diiriye Guure, i.e. the Sayid', i.e. Mohammed Abdullah Hassan.

Bishop Absalom is spelt as the source spells it (usually Absalon). The Viking slave trade to the Islamic world (Volga route, dirham hoards 786-1009) left out: the entry already names it. In 1043 Hallvard Vebjørnsson was killed defending a thrall woman and later canonised as Saint Hallvard; left out for length.
Heading 'Reign' avoided: she was a queen consort whose role is uncertain.

Article dates his death c. 628 or 630 (reign 618-628 in its first line); entry: murdered around 630. No year given. Article: scholars believe the khagan Xuanzang met at Suyab was Tong Yabghu, but Gao and La Vaissière argue it was his son Si Yabghu; the entry states it was Tong. Left out.
Kim died on 2 December 1953; the article says nothing more of his last years.

The article states the Confederacy was 'de facto independent' after the treaty, then reports that 20th-century literature finds the view of the treaty as a step to de facto independence untenable. The entry says 'effectively independent'. The text gives only the attributed historiography, without a verdict of its own. Short article: the text is near the lower limit.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance beyond the entry; it also contradicts itself on where the treaty was signed (after negotiations at Breslau, then 'actually signed in Berlin') Article lead: signed 11 June 1742 following negotiations at Breslau; Content section: 'actually signed in Berlin'.
